At the same time, the Company strengthened its SUV portfolio, sustained export growth and expanded its multi-powertrain creating, fresh momentum in its growth trajectory. Maruti Suzuki India Limited | Annual Integrated Report 2025-26 5 Maruti Suzuki India Limited (hereafter referred to as ‘MSIL ’ or ‘the Company’) is pleased to present its 45th Annual Report for FY 2025-26. This Report intends to serve as a concise communication about the Company’s thoughts on business, governance, performance (financial and non-financial) and prospects in the context of its external environment. Approach to Reporting Independent Assurance The financial information in this report has undergone independent assurance by Price Waterhouse Chartered Accountants LLP. Bureau Veritas India Pvt Ltd independently verified some of the essential non-financial disclosures, including BRSR. Reporting Framework The Integrated Reporting Framework (referred to as the 'Framework') developed by the International Integrated Reporting Council (IIRC) serves as the basis of this Report. The financial information presented in this Report complies with financial and statutory data requirements

(IIRC) serves as the basis of this Report. The financial information presented in this Report complies with financial and statutory data requirements of the Companies Act, 2013 (including the rules made thereunder), Indian Accounting Standards, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, and the Secretarial Standards. The Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) standards are the basis of the non-financial information presented in this Report. Additionally, this Report aligns with the Ten Principles of the 'United Nations Global Compact (UNGC)' and the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct (NGRBC) issued by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Government of India. Scope and Boundary The ‘reporting period’ is from 1st April 2025 to 31st March 2026. Pursuant to the amalgamation of Suzuki Motor Gujarat Private Limited (SMG) (hereinafter referred to as the Hansalpur facility) with Maruti Suzuki India Limited (MSIL),

This report covers the manufacturing facilities at Gurugram, Manesar, Hansalpur and Kharkhoda, Research and Development (R&D) facilities at Gurugram and Rohtak, Head Office at New Delhi, regional, zonal and area offices across India, sales and distribution facilities and stockyards. Company Profile Maruti Suzuki India Limited was established in 1981. A joint venture agreement was signed between the Government of India and Suzuki Motor Corporation (SMC), Japan in 1982. The Company became a subsidiary of SMC in 2002. In terms of production volume and sales, the Company is now SMC's largest subsidiary. As of 31st March 2026, SMC holds 58.53% of its equity stake. It is a public limited Company, and its shares are traded on the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). The Company is the market leader of Passenger Vehicles (PVs) in India and is also the country’s largest exporter of PVs. In FY 2025-26, the Company posted its highest-ever total sales, surpassing the milestone of 2 million units for the third year in a row. The Company is the first among PV manufacturers in India to achieve this milestone. Brief outline on CSR policy of the company The Company’s Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) initiatives are in the areas of Community Development, Skill Development and Road Safety. Company focuses on a few CSR programmes rather than spreading resources thin over several projects. Under the Community Development theme, the Company is committed to improving the well-being of the community by implementing social projects in designated villages around company’s facilities and local communities. To create a positive and meaningful impact on the lives of communities, the projects are undertaken to strengthen the common community infrastructure and improve health, education, water, and sanitation services, ensuring allround development. Standout examples include a multispecialty tertiary care hospital and a modern CBSE school in Gujarat, and holistic village development initiatives targeting ultra-local problems in the designated villages, significantly improving the lives of local residents. any has expanded its focus to address critical social priorities such as anemia reduction, promotion of menstrual hygiene among school children, large -scale tree plantation, establishment of STEM laboratories, and development of school libraries. The Company supports the measures to popularise the usage of Fermented Organic Manure (FOM) produced by biogas plants across India among the farmers. The project is implemented in phases including research on FOM, extension work comprising on-field demonstration & farmers connect program. Fermented Organic Manure (FOM) aligns with multiple SDGs and offers multiple benefits, including improved soil health, reduction in usage of chemical fertilisers, curb stubble burning, reduce the greenhouse gas emission, generate rural employment opportunities across the value chain, etc. contributing to sustainable agricultural development. sustainable agricultural development. Through Skill Development initiatives, the Company focuses on skill development and employability enhancement of youth, aligned with industry requirements. The Japan India Institute for Manufacturing (JIM), the company’s flagship skill development institute, is a key institute for vocational skill development that trains the youth in vocational courses through the latest technology tools, industry exposure through on-the-job training and shop-floor practices based on Japanese manufacturing methods. Through these initiatives, advanced labs are being set up, and industry relevant training is being provided to ITI trainers and students, aiming to build a workforce ready for the manufacturing industry. Background and EY’s Approach for the Impact Assessment EY conducted an independent impact assessment of Maruti Suzuki India Limited’s (MSIL) CSR initiatives across the areas of Community Development, Skill Development, and Road Safety. A combination of primary research (interviews, FGDs, surveys), field observations, and secondary analysis were used for the study. Given the nature of MSIL ’s CSR portfolio, the assessment adopted a time-slice approach, which focuses on assessing the most relevant and observable outcomes at the current stage of a project’s lifecycle while recognising that long-term impact develops progressively over time. Several interventions, including Village Development, Popularisation of FOM, Zydus Sitapur Hospital, Maruti Suzuki Podar Learn School, Japan India Institute of Manufacturing (JIM), and ITI Upgradation programmes, are

on of FOM, Zydus Sitapur Hospital, Maruti Suzuki Podar Learn School, Japan India Institute of Manufacturing (JIM), and ITI Upgradation programmes, are designed to drive longterm systemic change. Accordingly, the assessment focused on foundational and intermediate outcomes such as improved access to services, increased service utilisation, institutional strengthening, and stakeholder confidence. The assessment adopted a mixed-method approach, combining quantitative and qualitative techniques, with a strong emphasis on qualitative inquiry to capture stakeholder experiences, perceptions, and contextual factors. In-depth interviews, focus group discussions, and field observations complemented quantitative evidence to provide a comprehensive understanding of programme progress and outcomes. However, a significant proportion of the outcomes observed during the assessment were qualitative in nature, including enhanced community trust, behavioural changes, and improved workplace readiness.

The assessment also highlighted certain considerations related to outcome measurements across complex social development programmes. Several intended outcomes, such as reductions in road accidents, long-term livelihood improvements, enhanced educational attainment, and improved soil health, require sustained implementation and longer observation periods before they can be comprehensively assessed. In addition, outcomes such as behavioural change, trust, and community satisfaction remain inherently complex and often require qualitative approaches alongside conventional quantitative measurement techniques. To complement traditional assessment methods, EY undertook an impact video documentation exercise across selected project locations. The exercise provided valuable insights into beneficiary experiences, community perspectives, and

It enabled the documentation of lived experiences, institutional improvements, and stakeholder perceptions that are often difficult to capture through quantitative indicators and served as an important visual record of programme outcomes and community impact. The study also generated important learnings for strengthening future impact measurement efforts. Going forward, impact assessments can be further strengthened through robust baseline studies, projectspecific outcome frameworks, periodic outcome tracking, and longitudinal monitoring of beneficiaries. As programmes continue to mature, future assessments may increasingly focus on measuring longer-term social, economic, and behavioural outcomes alongside indicators related to access, utilisation, and institutional

Overall, the assessment indicates that MSIL ’s CSR initiatives are contributing to stronger institutions, improved access to essential services, enhanced employability, and increased stakeholder confidence across project locations. The findings provide evidence of progress across the assessed interventions while highlighting the importance of continued monitoring, evaluation, and evidence generation to better understand and capture longer-term programme outcomes as these initiatives evolve. 2. Annexure - C Commodity price risk or foreign exchange risk and hedging activities Annexure - 1 Commodities Price Risk Management and Hedge Policy 1.0 Background Maruti Suzuki India Limited (MSIL) for producing cars needs to purchase large volumes of basic commodities like steel, aluminium directly and indirectly and consume high quantities of copper and lead being used by its vendors for supplying components. Apart from these basic metals, significant quantities of Precious Group Metals like Platinum, Palladium and Rhodium as well as other commodities like plastics, High speed diesel (HSD) etc., are consumed. Due to high volume usage of the above-mentioned commodities in manufacturing cars and very high price volatility, which is being witnessed in last couple of

high volume usage of the above-mentioned commodities in manufacturing cars and very high price volatility, which is being witnessed in last couple of years, Company is exposed to severe commodity price risk directly as well as indirectly. These commodities are either being purchased from suppliers directly at mutually negotiated rates or the price is settled with suppliers, who manufacture these components for MSIL using these commodities, at monthly/quarterly settled prices based on prevalent market trends. Since these commodities and components are not purchased under a fixed price contract, the cost of the raw material input is variable. 2.0 Commodities Price Risk Management Objective and Strategies The commodities price risk management objective of the Company is to hedge the risk of changes in the commodity prices procured directly or indirectly (i.e., procured by component supplier). Since the fluctuations in commodity prices have severe impact on financials of the Company,

ctly or indirectly (i.e., procured by component supplier). Since the fluctuations in commodity prices have severe impact on financials of the Company, hedging provides stability to the financial performance by estimating the amount of future cash flows and reducing volatility. The Company shall follow a consistent policy of mitigating the commodities price risk by undertaking following strategies: I. Bundling of commodity sourcing Under this strategy, the Company shall negotiate with suppliers bundling its in house requirement with its vendor requirement to get a better price for different commodities based on large consolidated volume. II. Bundling of Suzuki Motor Corporation’s (SMC ) subsidiaries sourcing This strategy allows the Company to bundle the commodity sourcing for the SMC subsidiaries present in India in order to get better pricing for all the SMC group companies in India. III. Commodity Grade Standardisation & Substitution The Company shall undertake grade standardisation

ricing for all the SMC group companies in India. III. Commodity Grade Standardisation & Substitution The Company shall undertake grade standardisation across various categories of commodities to the extent possible like in the case of steel and plastic products so as to optimise the costs. The Company shall also change raw material grades to cheaper grades without affecting product performance e.g. in the case of steel from IF to EDD grade. IV. Yield Improvement The Company shall continuously under take yield improvement activities across various commodities like in the case of plastic products and electrical components, etc., done so far. V. Commodity price risk hedging MSIL shall follow a consistent policy of mitigating commodities price risk by entering into appropriate hedging instruments as considered necessary from time to time. Depending on the future outlook on commodity prices, the Company may keep the exposures un-hedged or hedge only a part of the total exposure. The

ime. Depending on the future outlook on commodity prices, the Company may keep the exposures un-hedged or hedge only a part of the total exposure. The Company shall not enter into commodity hedging transactions for speculative purposes i.e. without any actual/anticipated underlying exposure. The Company shall strictly observe the rules and regulations laid down by RBI for undertaking the commodities price risk hedging. 3.0 Commodities Permitted for Hedging The Company may hedge commodities price risk on all the commodities being purchased directly or indirectly e.g. Aluminium, Copper, Lead, Platinum, Rhodium, Palladium, Steel, Plastic, etc., wherever possible and permissible under the applicable rules and regulations to enable fixing the sourcing costs.

ith reference to financial statements. Meaning of Internal Financial Controls with reference to financial statements 6. A company's internal financial control with reference to financial statements is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company's internal financial control with reference to financial statements includes those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with

in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorisations of management and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, use, or disposition of the company's assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements.
